title: A central role for dietary sugars in human evolution.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Europe PMC core record for DOI 10.1126/science.aed8437 (PMID 42561068): publication type is 'Review', isOpenAccess=N, inPMC=N, hasSuppl=N, hasData=N, no text-mined accessions. Europe PMC datalinks endpoint returned 0 hits. Zenodo search on the title/DOI returned 0 records; Dryad search returned only one unrelated dataset (ADH7 across mammals, doi:10.5061/dryad.t4b8gtj6r). The publisher page science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aed8437 returned HTTP 403 (paywalled). The University of Glasgow repository record (eprints 392470) says 'Full text not currently available' and lists no downloadable files, though it flags that a data availability statement exists.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: Everything about the content: that the authors model macronutrient distribution across 4 million years of hominin evolution and conclude sugars supplied >25% of dietary energy. This comes from the abstract only; I could not read the methods, the data availability statement, or any table.

a1_downloadable.note: No data file is reachable. The article itself is paywalled (HTTP 403 from science.org), there is no PubMed Central copy, Europe PMC reports no supplementary files and no data links, and searches of Zenodo and Dryad on the DOI and title found nothing. The only repository record (University of Glasgow) hosts no files. This is a hard A1 failure: nothing to open.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: There is no table at all, so no label column. The quantity of interest (percent of dietary energy from sugar for a given hominin at a given time) is an output of the authors' own literature-parameterised calculation, not a measured column anyone could download.

a3_inputs_present.note: No input features exist in machine-readable form. Any features (brain mass, body mass, basal metabolic rate, food availability by habitat) would have to be re-extracted by hand from the cited palaeoanthropology and nutrition literature.

a4_units_stated.note: Units (kcal per day, percent of energy, grams) are presumably stated in the figures, but there is no units column because there is no data file to inspect.

a5_enough_rows.note: Not verified because no file exists, but the ceiling is structural: the paper spans roughly a dozen hominin taxa or time slices over 4 million years. That is one to two orders of magnitude below the ~1,500-row bar, and no amount of reformatting changes it.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: <1 MB if the figures were digitised by hand
a6_fits_laptop.note: Size is the one thing that is not a problem; the material is tiny. This does not rescue the candidate.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Cannot be checked. There is no download, no application programming interface (API) record of files, and no stated row count to compare against.

a8_label_provenance.note: The headline quantity ('sugars provided >25% of dietary energy') is the output of the authors' own nutritional-geometry model, computed from the same literature-derived parameters that would serve as features. That is leakage by construction plus model distillation in one step: the exact pair of failures A8 is written to catch.

honest_claim_h3: No claim is possible: there is no dataset behind this review, and the one number it reports is the output of the authors' own calculation rather than a measurement.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use body and brain size and habitat of extinct human ancestors to predict the share of their diet that was sugar.
plain_idea.train_on: Would need one row per hominin species or time slice, with brain mass, body mass, estimated daily energy need and habitat type. Verified count: zero rows available; the realistic ceiling is roughly a dozen taxa across 4 million years.
plain_idea.predict: Percentage of dietary energy from sugars. The 'true answer' is not a measurement at all: it is computed by the authors' nutritional-geometry model from the same literature-derived parameters that would be the features.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: It would not be. Palaeodiet reconstruction matters to palaeoanthropologists and nutrition researchers, but with a dozen rows and a model-generated target, a machine learning model would only re-derive the authors' own arithmetic and learn nothing about biology.

label_elsewhere.sources: None found. Searched Zenodo and Dryad on the DOI and title and found no deposit; no public resource records 'percent of dietary energy from sugar' for extinct hominins. Related but non-joinable measurements exist (stable carbon and nitrogen isotope ratios in fossil tooth enamel, dental microwear texture databases), but these measure different quantities on different units of analysis.
label_elsewhere.join_key: none (hominin species name as free text at best)
label_elsewhere.why: The target exists only as this paper's modelled output, so there is no external labelled set to train on or validate against.

ml_idea: None viable. The only machine learning framing — predict modelled sugar share from hominin body and brain parameters — would be fitting a regression to a dozen points whose target was itself computed from those same parameters.

effort.compute_note: Not estimated: there is no dataset to size. Compute was never the constraint here.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Query Europe PMC for the publication type and supplementary-file flags. It returns 'Review', hasSuppl=N, hasData=N in one call, which kills the candidate in under a minute.

verdict_reason: This is a paywalled Science Review article, not a data paper. Part A1 fails outright: no supplementary files in Europe PMC, no data links, nothing on Zenodo or Dryad, and the publisher page returns 403, so there is nothing to open. A2, A3 and A5 would fail too — there is no table, no feature columns, and at most a dozen hominin time slices in the whole 4-million-year span. A8 is the deepest problem: the headline '>25% of dietary energy from sugar' is the output of the authors' own nutritional-geometry model computed from the very parameters that would be the features, so any model fitted to it would distill their arithmetic rather than learn biology.
